issue: Can a district court grant an open-ended continuance under the Speedy Trial Act's ends-of-justice provision, and if so, what limits apply (such as a reasonable length or periodic reevaluation)?

sides.position: Open-ended ends-of-justice continuances are not prohibited, provided they are reasonable in length, and a continuance of any substantial length must be adequately justified by the circumstances.
cases: United States v. Rush, 738 F.2d 497 (1st Cir. 1984)
United States v. Lattany, 982 F.2d 866 (3d Cir. 1992)
United States v. Jones, 56 F.3d 581 (5th Cir. 1995)
United States v. Spring, 80 F.3d 1450 (10th Cir. 1996)
United States v. Harris-Franklin, No. 24-2451 (8th Cir. 2025)

sides.position: An open-ended continuance is permissible only if it is effectively limited in time, for example because the district court periodically reevaluates it; a continuance not reevaluated during the period, with no case progress, does not satisfy the Act.
cases: United States v. Harris-Franklin, No. 24-2451 (8th Cir. 2025)

this_court: The Eighth Circuit takes the restrictive position: an open-ended continuance must be effectively limited, such as by regular reevaluation, and the continuance here was not, so the Speedy Trial Act was violated.
quote: Our sister “circuits have split over whether a district court may grant an openended continuance under § 3161(h)([7])(A).”
cite: United States v. Markhel Harris-Franklin, No. 24-2451 (8th Cir. 2025)
